rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-2.3 and 3 (Figs. 3-8, Tables 3-4) report the authors' own ISAREG simulation runs of four irrigation scheduling alternatives for maize on a vertisol at Pustren over 1970-1992 and for hypothetical 2005-2030 precipitation scenarios.
rows.notes: The study does apply a scheduling simulation model (ISAREG, FAO56-based) to search irrigation schedules that cope with drought and climate uncertainty, which matches the passage. However, every result on the claimed effect (irrigation demand, soil water, relative yield decrease under the alternatives and scenarios) is model output; no simulated output is compared with field measurements in this paper. Model calibration/validation is only cited from a former study (Popova et al. 2006a), and the climate scenarios are explicitly hypothetical, not predictions. Under the rule that simulations count only when checked against observations in the study itself, Q2 is answered no; this is a judgement call since the model was validated for the same site in the earlier paper. Had Q2 been yes: Q4 could be yes (simulated available soil water as intermediate variable, Figs. 4,5,8), Q7 yes (MAD constrained by vertisol cracking threshold; last irrigation date; need for stress-tolerant hybrids), Q8 yes (record length insufficient, scenarios not predictions, cannot select a best alternative, economics not assessed), Q3/Q5/Q6/Q9 no (single site and soil, one crop, no dispersion on results).

notes: Full text appears complete. Single-site (Pustren, Thrace plain) simulation study with one soil, one crop (two maize hybrids); the only dispersion statistic reported is an 80% confidence interval for ETo as an input, not for the scheduling results.
